newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia's Chiluba looks set for tough second term.
newsitem.headline: Zambia's Chiluba looks set for tough second term.

text.p: Zambia's President Frederick Chiluba has ensured himself a second term in office after Monday's elections but may pay dearly for the way he did it, diplomats say.
Chiluba's Movement for Multiparty Democracy (MMD) pushed through constitutional changes this year that bar his main rival and predecessor, Kenneth Kaunda, from challenging him.
Four presidential rivals still in the race have little hope of defeating the former trade unionist who ended 27 years of Kaunda rule in 1991 with an astounding 76 percent of the vote.

But barring Kaunda on the grounds his parents were born abroad has sowed the seeds both for political strife and -- after Western donors froze aid in protest -- of economic decay in the impoverished and debt-ridden southern African state.
Chiluba, 53, has alienated South Africa, the regional superpower, by rejecting President Nelson Mandela's last-minute plea for a postponement of the vote and dialogue with Kaunda.
Ironically, most political analysts say the born-again Christian would have won even with Kaunda standing, but it seems he, or a powerful MMD circle, did not want the risk.

Frosty relations with the neighbours, in a now peaceful region trying to show the way forward for Africa, will be bad enough but the block on aid to help the balance of payments could cause Chiluba serious trouble, they said.
His free-market policies, abolishing of exchange controls and privatisation drive won the praise of the World Bank, but austerity measures have made life tougher for many Zambians.
Servicing a $6.4 billion debt alone will be hard.
Chiluba rose through trade union ranks to defeat Kaunda, leader for 27 years since independence from Britain, with a call for democracy, economic reform and clean government.
But Western diplomats said the rot set in a couple of years ago, when attacks on opposition press increased and the MMD's commitment to democracy began to look less firm.
Chiluba has also had to fend off persistent claims by the opposition, police sources and foreign media that senior party members are involved in drug trafficking around the region.
An energetic and charismatic politician who stands about five feet (1.5 metres) tall, Frederick Jacob Titus Chiluba was born at Kitwe on the Copperbelt area in April 1943.
He left school early but continued studies on his own while he worked as an accountant before devoting himself to politics.
His trade union career started in 1967 as a shop steward. He rose through union ranks and became chairman of the Zambian Confederation of Trade Unions in 1974.
He married Vera Tembo in 1968 and they have five boys and four girls.
